Nonpartisan analyses for California’s policymakers to improve programs and services for all Californians.
Our office evaluates complex problems and recommends actionable solutions to help government provide efficient and equitable access to services for all Californians.
Our work is independent, nonpartisan, and results directly from the facts and data we collect.
When decision-makers act on our recommendations, real change happens. Because of our work, children have improved access to preventive health care, more California students are protected at our institutions of higher learning, there’s increased accountability in the spending of public funds, and small businesses can count on more fair equitable protections for California’s growing cannabis industry.
How Our Work Begins
Our audits and investigations are launched from different sources.
The Legislature
Legislators concerned about a program or agency can request a performance/policy evaluation through the bipartisan Joint Legislative Audit Committee (JLAC). The California State Auditor’s Office is involved from the beginning of this process. We review a legislator’s request for an audit and are available to answer questions when the request is formally made to JLAC. You can find more information on the JLAC audit request process on their Frequently Asked Questions (https://legaudit.assembly.ca.gov/content/faq) website.
If JLAC approves the request, our audit work begins. In this phase of the process, we gather the facts and dive into the details. Once we have analyzed all the evidence, we issue a public report. Everything we do is confidential until we publish our final report.
After we publish our reports, the Legislature may hold hearings and pass legislation to address the weaknesses we identified.
Whistleblower Tips
The California Whistleblower Protection Act authorizes the California State Auditor to receive whistleblower tips from state employees and members of the public who wish to report improper state government activity. Our office works diligently to investigate whistleblower tips of fraud, waste, and abuse of taxpayer funds, and provide recommendations to agencies to remedy these issues. All investigations are completely confidential unless the California State Auditor issues a public report.
For more on this process visit our Whistleblower webpage (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/whistleblower/) and be sure to check out our Whistleblower Frequently Asked Questions (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/whistleblower/#frequently-asked-questions).
State Laws
The California Legislature may pass legislation requiring the California State Auditor’s Office to conduct audits of programs, agencies, and governments, either on a one-time basis or continually. Examples of this legisation:
Alternative Whistleblower System Regulations: 2 CCR § 61300-61320
Redistricting Regulations: 2 CCR § 60800-60863
State High Risk Program: 2 CCR § 61000-61024
Local Government High Risk Program: 2 CCR § 61100-61140
California Healthcare, Research, and Prevention Tobacco Tax Act of 2016: 2 CCR § 61200-61240 (https://govt.westlaw.com/calregs/Browse/Home/California/CaliforniaCodeofRegulations?guid=I0986F16512064ABB8427E91C01DA1EB6&originationContext=documenttoc&transitionType=Default&contextData=(sc.Default))
High-Risk Issues
As required by Government Code section 8546.5, our office operates the High-Risk program to improve the operation of state government. We identify, audit, and recommend improvements to state agencies and statewide issues at high risk for waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement, or for having major challenges associated with their economy, efficiency, or effectiveness. Some current issues include state management of COVID-19 federal funds, water infrastructure, and information security. See the California State Auditor’s latest 2025 High-Risk report (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/2025-601/).

Performance & Policy Evaluations
As part of performance/policy evaluations—also known as performance audits—we collect evidence and find the truth. We use that truth to craft recommendations so that those in power can best serve the people they represent. Performance/policy evaluations involve systematically comparing what should be happening to what is happening. Our analyses and recommendations are objective, independent, nonpartisan, and based on evidence. We ultimately determine whether government agencies are efficient, effective, fulfilling their missions, and complying with the law. Our office is also responsible for audits that are mandated by state law, such as our annual review of the state judicial system.
Investigations into Improper Governmental Activities
If state agencies or employees are acting improperly, our team investigates them and develops reports to hold them accountable. Under the California Whistleblower Protection Act, we determine whether allegations of improper governmental activities are true and follow up to make sure they implement our recommendations for corrective action. We conduct investigations in response to complaints received from state employees, members of the public, or on our own initiative. We receive complaints by telephone, mail, fax, and through this website. Complainants have a right to remain confidential. More information can be found on our Whistleblower Hotline webpage (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/whistleblower/)
Financial & Compliance Audits
With billions of dollars in federal funding on the line, determining whether California’s financial statements are presented fairly is critical work. Each year, our staff conducts our annual audit of the State’s financial statements to ensure that California can receive funding that supports infrastructure, schools, and other public services. This audit—known as the Single Audit (https://information.auditor.ca.gov/stimulus)—is among the largest in the world and encompasses our evaluation of California’s financial statements, financial reporting safeguards, and compliance with laws, rules, and requirements. It satisfies the federal requirements for an independent financial audit and reviews the State’s compliance with federal program requirements.
Data Analytics
Our data analysts delve into large datasets to provide easily understood and visualized analyses to auditors, the Legislature, and the public. Our office can quickly clean and synthesize data to point in the right direction to address problems facing Californians.
State High-Risk Program
We investigate statewide issues and improve the operation of state government by identifying, auditing, and recommending improvements. We target state programs at high risk for waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement. We also audit programs experiencing major challenges associated with their economy, efficiency, or effectiveness.
Our Mission, Authority, & Standards
1
Our Mission
Our mission is to provide objective evaluations and effective solutions that enhance the transparency, accountability, and performance of California government for the people it serves. We follow the highest standards to provide stakeholders with reliable answers to problems in California government. We gather evidence to understand what an agency or program is meant to achieve, to determine whether it is falling short, and articulate what performance means for the people it serves.
2
Our Authority
State laws mandate our office be independent of the executive branch and legislative control. The California State Auditor is the only entity that has, by statute, full access to all records, accounts, correspondence, property, and other files of any publicly created entity, including state agencies, cities, counties, school districts, and special districts.
3
Our Standards
The California State Auditor’s Office conducts all performance and policy evaluations—also known as performance audits—in accordance with audit standards issued by the U.S. Comptroller General’s Government Accountability Office (GAO), including standards that we must follow as an independent auditor. To preserve the independence of our office and to ensure the receipt of federal funds, state law requires the State Auditor to follow those standards that explicitly free the auditor from control by the executive branch.

Peer Review Results
Each audit organization performing audits in accordance with generally accepted government auditing standards must have an external peer review performed by reviewers independent of the audit organization being reviewed at least once every three years.
The California State Auditor’s Office received its last peer review rating of pass in 2026, included in the 2026 Peer Review Report (http://www.auditor.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/NSAA-CSA-2026-Peer-Review-Report.pdf).
Accessible 2026 report available (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/2026-nsaa-external-peer-review-results/)

Our data analysts delve into large datasets to provide easily understood and visualized analyses to auditors, the Legislature, and the public. Our office can quickly clean and synthesize data to point in the right direction to address problems facing Californians.
State High-Risk Program
We investigate statewide issues and improve the operation of state government by identifying, auditing, and recommending improvements. We target state programs at high risk for waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement. We also audit programs experiencing major challenges associated with their economy, efficiency, or effectiveness.
Our Mission, Authority, & Standards
1
Our Mission
Our mission is to provide objective evaluations and effective solutions that enhance the transparency, accountability, and performance of California government for the people it serves. We follow the highest standards to provide stakeholders with reliable answers to problems in California government. We gather evidence to understand what an agency or program is meant to achieve, to determine whether it is falling short, and articulate what performance means for the people it serves.
2
Our Authority
State laws mandate our office be independent of the executive branch and legislative control. The California State Auditor is the only entity that has, by statute, full access to all records, accounts, correspondence, property, and other files of any publicly created entity, including state agencies, cities, counties, school districts, and special districts.
3
Our Standards
The California State Auditor’s Office conducts all performance and policy evaluations—also known as performance audits—in accordance with audit standards issued by the U.S. Comptroller General’s Government Accountability Office (GAO), including standards that we must follow as an independent auditor. To preserve the independence of our office and to ensure the receipt of federal funds, state law requires the State Auditor to follow those standards that explicitly free the auditor from control by the executive branch.

Frequently Asked Questions About Proposition 41
Q: What does Prop 41 do?
A: Prop 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct public performance and financial audits of programs funded by proposed new taxes, bringing government transparency and accountability to spending decisions before voters make them.
Californians pay some of the highest taxes in the country - on top of our high cost of living. Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. We deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Proposition 41 (2026) puts independent audits and measurable outcomes at the center of how California funds programs with new tax dollars, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Q: Does Prop 41 raise taxes?
A: No. Prop 41 does not create or increase any taxes - it protects taxpayers' interests by:
1) Identifying shortcomings in programs and recommending fixes, to help deliver better results for our taxes;
Reducing the waste and fraud that have cost California taxpayers billions of dollars in recent years; and
Requires all taxes to comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - including its requirement that excess revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Prop 41 ensures taxpayers get better results, not just a bigger tax bill.
Q: How do the audits work?
Proposition 41 requires the independent California State Auditor to review programs that would be funded by a new or higher special tax proposed to California voters. The first review happens before the tax reaches the ballot. Once a special tax initiative collects 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify, the State Auditor audits each program that would receive the money, looking at whether the program is achieving its goals, how well it spends its dollars, and where fraud, waste, or abuse may exist. A summary of the findings is printed in the Voter Information Guide so voters can read it before they vote. If a new special tax is approved by voters, the State Auditor reviews the funded programs again every four years and invites public input.
The audits produce findings and recommendations, and both are public. Decisions about funding stay with voters and the Legislature, as they are today, and the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst Office notes that acting on the recommendations "could result in savings or improved
services at existing funding levels." A program funded by a new special tax is reviewed before any change to its funding is made. For a full walkthrough, see the our explainer here (https://www.yesonprop41.org/how-audits-work) .
Q: Who conducts the audits?
A: The audits are conducted by California's independent State Auditor, the state's nonpartisan fiscal watchdog, and shared broadly with the public, including in the Voter Information Guide. The financial and performance audits must:
Track all program spending and assess whether it's achieving its intended outcomes;
Determine whether programs have sufficient oversight and accountability;
Identify areas of waste, fraud and abuse; and,
Recommend how future waste and fraud can be avoided and how programs can be made more effective.
Under Prop 41, the Auditor is required to review programs funded by proposed new tax measures before voters cast their ballots and conduct ongoing audits if those measures are approved.
Q: What happens if an audit finds problems?
A: If the State Auditor identifies concerns about oversight, accountability or program performance, those findings are included in the Voter Information Guide so voters can make a more informed decision.
If a measure is approved, future audits continue evaluating how funds are spent, identify areas for improvement, and recommend ways to make programs more effective over time - so that programs are held accountable to the people who pay for them: taxpayers.
The audit doesn't decide whether a measure passes or fails; it gives voters independent information before they cast their ballot.
Q: What does Prop 41 mean for education, healthcare and other public programs?
A: Every tax dollar we waste is a dollar that could actually help someone. Prop 41 is built to sustain fiscal discipline alongside public investment. It does not cut or eliminate funding for education, healthcare or other public services, and it helps ensure that programs funded by taxpayers are transparent, accountable and delivering results. We deserve better services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Prop 41 requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, like homelessness (https://www.yesonprop41.org/homelessness) , so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Q: Does Prop 41 make it harder for initiatives to qualify for the ballot?
A: No. Prop 41 does not change the initiative process or prevent measures from qualifying for the ballot. Supporters can still gather signatures, qualify initiatives and campaign for their proposals just as they do today.
The difference is that under Prop 41, programs to be funded by new taxes are assessed before voters cast their ballot. The Auditor's findings must be posted in the Voter Information Guide, so voters have access to independent information about how programs are being managed and whether they actually need more funding. Voters deserve the ability to make informed decisions about new taxes without having to rely on information from special interests or politicians.
Q: Who pays for the audits?
A: If a tax measure is approved, the cost of the required audits is paid from the revenues generated by that measure. If voters reject the measure, the audit costs are paid through the state's General Fund.
Many statewide tax measures raise hundreds of millions - or even billions - of dollars over time. Prop 41 ensures a small investment in independent oversight helps taxpayers know whether those dollars are being spent effectively and producing the results promised.
Q: Who supports Prop 41?
Prop 41 is backed by a board coalition of small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, accountants, and auditing experts. Endorsers include the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, former State Controller Steve Westly, former California Auditor General Tom Hayes, the NAACP California-Hawaii State Conference, the California Alliance of Seniors, the California Chamber of Commerce, the California Farm Bureau, the California Taxpayers Association, the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, along with dozens of local chambers, taxpayer associations, and regional economic partnerships across the state.
Endorsements also include Democratic organizations and officials. The Chinese American Democratic Club, the San Bernardino Young Democrats, and the Sacramento State College Democrats have endorsed Prop 41, as has Steve Westly, a Democrat who served as State Controller. Local officials who have endorsed include Riverside County Auditor-Controller Ben Benoit and council members and mayors from across California. The full and current list of endorsers is at yesonprop41.org/endorsements (https://www.yesonprop41.org/endorsements) .
Q: How does Prop 41 strengthen taxpayer protections?
A: Prop 41 requires all future state tax measures to comply with California's voter-approved constitutional spending limit. That means future measures must follow the same constitutional rules that already apply to state spending including the requirement that excess revenues be refunded to taxpayers when the spending limit is exceeded.
Prop 41 provides for consistent application of the spending limit, so future state tax measures follow the same constitutional rules that already govern state spending, including the requirement that excess revenues be refunded to taxpayers.

Endorsement: Yes on Propositions 41 and 42 to limit taxation in California

By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 21, 2026 at 2:39 PM PDT | UPDATED: September 21, 2026 at 2:56 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
The most hotly debated initiative on the November ballot is Proposition 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires. As this Editorial Board opined (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/) in our opposition, the union-created Billionaire Tax Act would send a dangerous message to current and future entrepreneurs, and “have a chilling effect on investment.”
But two closely related measures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://www.bakersfield.com/opinion/our-view/our-view-vote-no-on-propositions-40-41-42-tax-propositions-hurt-state-californians/article_1c8492b8-5fb9-4897-9f1c-c9ba56460e0d.amp.html) , have received much less attention — partly because they’re so complicated. By adding related measures to the ballot, opponents of Prop. 40 are hoping that voters approve one of these alternatives that will derail Prop. 40. Because these two measures have elements that contradict Prop. 40, the one that gets the highest vote totals (if voters OK them all) would go into effect.
Adding similar-sounding measures also muddies the waters, thus increasing the likelihood that confused voters vote “no” on all of them — thus accomplishing the main goal of stopping the billionaires’ tax. But our goal isn’t to map out political strategies (https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/nash-game/) . It’s a worthy effort to try to stop a disastrous new tax scheme.
Besides their intended purpose of blocking Prop. 40, the measures could protect taxpayers for years to come.
Specifically, Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. Those audits, which must be completed before the initiative appears on the ballot, would be required to identify ways that such programs could cut annual costs by 10%, per an analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026) from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
While Prop. 40 exempts itself from state spending limits, Prop. 41 also requires new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit (https://www.sheehystrategygroup.com/news/2026/3/9/californias-state-appropriations-limit-gann-limit) — the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year. The state has passed a number of workarounds over the years, but applying new revenues to this formula would potentially require the return of certain additional tax revenues to taxpayers (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41) and the earmarking of revenues to infrastructure.
Prop. 42 is more straightforward. Per theLAO (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), the initiative prohibits “new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.” California doesn’t currently tax the ownership of financial assets and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees), but the measure’s passage “could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.” It also limits imposition of retroactive taxes.
So would the Editorial Board support these measures even if they were standalone initiatives? The answers are unequivocal: Yes and yes.

Regarding Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) , California could use better audits of spending programs. It’s a good idea to identify ways to trim existing programs before shoveling more money their way. It is taxpayers’ money, after all. Requiring audits after election officials have collected only 25% of qualifying signatures imposes a relatively costly burden, but those expenses are a rounding error for any major program. We also believe the state should better live up to the terms of the Gann Limit.
Regarding Prop. 42 (https://yesonprop42.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=YesOn42&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24250385746&gbraid=0AAAABEi2smx27CdnofkbhPlt_FqIHXDrD&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHUyIfjJPNFkY5WqUynwZ9APOIPtTZDTa7v5_wEBmvD8nV21v3IkUbhoCCZ8QAvD_BwE) , we endorse its efforts to limit unreasonable future tax increases. G oing back and raising taxes on past earnings (as Prop. 40 does) before the new law was passed is unseemly. Opponents complain that it ties the hands of future Legislatures, but we’re totally fine with putting certain types of assets outside the revenuers’ grasp.
Vote yes on Propositions 41 and 42.

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California’s Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.

Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. California voters should know what Proposition 41 is about. Here is the truth | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 2, 2026 3:42 PM
Prop. 41 would mandate audits for voter-approved special taxes, add ongoing reviews every four years, and may undermine the one-time billionaire tax.
Viorika
Getty Images/iStockphoto
Proposition 41 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005690.html) is a constitutional amendment billed as a way to add transparency and accountability to ballot measures for special taxes.
Voters should beware. Prop. 41 is supported by Building a Better California, which is funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other CEOs and entrepreneurs. These people have created Prop. 41 and Proposition 42 to confuse voters. Why? They want to undermine Proposition 40, the so-called “billionaire tax” also on your ballot.
Perhaps the most controversial measure on your ballot,Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% wealth tax (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317269166.html) on California residents with more than $1 billion in total assets.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 41 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005690.html)
How could Prop. 41 invalidate Prop. 40? As The Bee wrote last week, “One of the most important provisions of Prop. 41 would ban taxes on or after Jan. 1, 2026, that are exempt from state spending limits.” That’s important because Prop. 40, as it is written is exempt from state spending limits.
So if Prop. 41 gets more “Yes” votes than a competing measure such as Prop. 40, the provisions of Prop. 41 would prevail over the provisions of Prop. 40, according to the California Constitution. We don’t believe enough voters understand this because while Prop. 40 has garnered a great deal of attention and debate, Prop. 41 has not.
This is why the collective editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee, (https://www.sacbee.com/)Modesto Bee (https://www.modbee.com/), Merced Sun-Star, (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/) Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) urges a “No” vote on Prop. 41. What’s insidious Prop. 41 is that it is presented as a good governance measure when it’s really about defeating Prop. 40. A majority of our board supported Prop. 40, but it wasn’t unanimous. We understand that it’s controversial to tax California’s most wealthy residents.
But as we wrote in our endorsement, “Billionaires have every right to fight a tax that could cost them billions. But voters should recognize the enormous political power that such wealth can buy and ask why so much of that power has been exercised through campaign committees rather than direct public engagement.”
Included in that power is the use of the initiative process to confuse voters with measures competing with Prop. 40. Voters should know that Prop. 41 has a specific target and is funded and supported by wealthy people with a financial stake in defeating Prop. 40.
We hope Californians vote “No” on Prop. 41.

2026 Peer Review results
Nonpartisan analyses for California’s policymakers to improve programs and services for all Californians.
Our office evaluates complex problems and recommends actionable solutions to help government provide efficient and equitable access to services for all Californians.
Our work is independent, nonpartisan, and results directly from the facts and data we collect.
When decision-makers act on our recommendations, real change happens. Because of our work, children have improved access to preventive health care, more California students are protected at our institutions of higher learning, there’s increased accountability in the spending of public funds, and small businesses can count on more fair equitable protections for California’s growing cannabis industry.
How Our Work Begins
Our audits and investigations are launched from different sources.
The Legislature
Legislators concerned about a program or agency can request a performance/policy evaluation through the bipartisan Joint Legislative Audit Committee (JLAC). The California State Auditor’s Office is involved from the beginning of this process. We review a legislator’s request for an audit and are available to answer questions when the request is formally made to JLAC. You can find more information on the JLAC audit request process on their Frequently Asked Questions (https://legaudit.assembly.ca.gov/content/faq) website.
If JLAC approves the request, our audit work begins. In this phase of the process, we gather the facts and dive into the details. Once we have analyzed all the evidence, we issue a public report. Everything we do is confidential until we publish our final report.
After we publish our reports, the Legislature may hold hearings and pass legislation to address the weaknesses we identified.
Whistleblower Tips
The California Whistleblower Protection Act authorizes the California State Auditor to receive whistleblower tips from state employees and members of the public who wish to report improper state government activity. Our office works diligently to investigate whistleblower tips of fraud, waste, and abuse of taxpayer funds, and provide recommendations to agencies to remedy these issues. All investigations are completely confidential unless the California State Auditor issues a public report.
For more on this process visit our Whistleblower webpage (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/whistleblower/) and be sure to check out our Whistleblower Frequently Asked Questions (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/whistleblower/#frequently-asked-questions).
State Laws
The California Legislature may pass legislation requiring the California State Auditor’s Office to conduct audits of programs, agencies, and governments, either on a one-time basis or continually. Examples of this legisation:
Alternative Whistleblower System Regulations: 2 CCR § 61300-61320
Redistricting Regulations: 2 CCR § 60800-60863
State High Risk Program: 2 CCR § 61000-61024
Local Government High Risk Program: 2 CCR § 61100-61140
California Healthcare, Research, and Prevention Tobacco Tax Act of 2016: 2 CCR § 61200-61240 (https://govt.westlaw.com/calregs/Browse/Home/California/CaliforniaCodeofRegulations?guid=I0986F16512064ABB8427E91C01DA1EB6&originationContext=documenttoc&transitionType=Default&contextData=(sc.Default))
High-Risk Issues
As required by Government Code section 8546.5, our office operates the High-Risk program to improve the operation of state government. We identify, audit, and recommend improvements to state agencies and statewide issues at high risk for waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement, or for having major challenges associated with their economy, efficiency, or effectiveness. Some current issues include state management of COVID-19 federal funds, water infrastructure, and information security. See the California State Auditor’s latest 2025 High-Risk report (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/2025-601/).
Areas of Expertise
Looking for a job with the California State Auditor?
Explore Careers (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/careers/)
Performance & Policy Evaluations
As part of performance/policy evaluations—also known as performance audits—we collect evidence and find the truth. We use that truth to craft recommendations so that those in power can best serve the people they represent. Performance/policy evaluations involve systematically comparing what should be happening to what is happening. Our analyses and recommendations are objective, independent, nonpartisan, and based on evidence. We ultimately determine whether government agencies are efficient, effective, fulfilling their missions, and complying with the law. Our office is also responsible for audits that are mandated by state law, such as our annual review of the state judicial system.
Investigations into Improper Governmental Activities
If state agencies or employees are acting improperly, our team investigates them and develops reports to hold them accountable. Under the California Whistleblower Protection Act, we determine whether allegations of improper governmental activities are true and follow up to make sure they implement our recommendations for corrective action. We conduct investigations in response to complaints received from state employees, members of the public, or on our own initiative. We receive complaints by telephone, mail, fax, and through this website. Complainants have a right to remain confidential. More information can be found on our Whistleblower Hotline webpage (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/whistleblower/)
Financial & Compliance Audits
With billions of dollars in federal funding on the line, determining whether California’s financial statements are presented fairly is critical work. Each year, our staff conducts our annual audit of the State’s financial statements to ensure that California can receive funding that supports infrastructure, schools, and other public services. This audit—known as the Single Audit (https://information.auditor.ca.gov/stimulus)—is among the largest in the world and encompasses our evaluation of California’s financial statements, financial reporting safeguards, and compliance with laws, rules, and requirements. It satisfies the federal requirements for an independent financial audit and reviews the State’s compliance with federal program requirements.
Data Analytics
Our data analysts delve into large datasets to provide easily understood and visualized analyses to auditors, the Legislature, and the public. Our office can quickly clean and synthesize data to point in the right direction to address problems facing Californians.
State High-Risk Program
We investigate statewide issues and improve the operation of state government by identifying, auditing, and recommending improvements. We target state programs at high risk for waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement. We also audit programs experiencing major challenges associated with their economy, efficiency, or effectiveness.
Our Mission, Authority, & Standards
1
Our Mission
Our mission is to provide objective evaluations and effective solutions that enhance the transparency, accountability, and performance of California government for the people it serves. We follow the highest standards to provide stakeholders with reliable answers to problems in California government. We gather evidence to understand what an agency or program is meant to achieve, to determine whether it is falling short, and articulate what performance means for the people it serves.
2
Our Authority
State laws mandate our office be independent of the executive branch and legislative control. The California State Auditor is the only entity that has, by statute, full access to all records, accounts, correspondence, property, and other files of any publicly created entity, including state agencies, cities, counties, school districts, and special districts.
3
Our Standards
The California State Auditor’s Office conducts all performance and policy evaluations—also known as performance audits—in accordance with audit standards issued by the U.S. Comptroller General’s Government Accountability Office (GAO), including standards that we must follow as an independent auditor. To preserve the independence of our office and to ensure the receipt of federal funds, state law requires the State Auditor to follow those standards that explicitly free the auditor from control by the executive branch.

Frequently Asked Questions About Proposition 41
Q: What does Prop 41 do?
A: Prop 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct public performance and financial audits of programs funded by proposed new taxes, bringing government transparency and accountability to spending decisions before voters make them.
Californians pay some of the highest taxes in the country - on top of our high cost of living. Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. We deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Proposition 41 (2026) puts independent audits and measurable outcomes at the center of how California funds programs with new tax dollars, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Q: Does Prop 41 raise taxes?
A: No. Prop 41 does not create or increase any taxes - it protects taxpayers' interests by:
1) Identifying shortcomings in programs and recommending fixes, to help deliver better results for our taxes;
Reducing the waste and fraud that have cost California taxpayers billions of dollars in recent years; and
Requires all taxes to comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - including its requirement that excess revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Prop 41 ensures taxpayers get better results, not just a bigger tax bill.
Q: How do the audits work?
Proposition 41 requires the independent California State Auditor to review programs that would be funded by a new or higher special tax proposed to California voters. The first review happens before the tax reaches the ballot. Once a special tax initiative collects 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify, the State Auditor audits each program that would receive the money, looking at whether the program is achieving its goals, how well it spends its dollars, and where fraud, waste, or abuse may exist. A summary of the findings is printed in the Voter Information Guide so voters can read it before they vote. If a new special tax is approved by voters, the State Auditor reviews the funded programs again every four years and invites public input.
The audits produce findings and recommendations, and both are public. Decisions about funding stay with voters and the Legislature, as they are today, and the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst Office notes that acting on the recommendations "could result in savings or improved
services at existing funding levels." A program funded by a new special tax is reviewed before any change to its funding is made. For a full walkthrough, see the our explainer here (https://www.yesonprop41.org/how-audits-work) .
Q: Who conducts the audits?
A: The audits are conducted by California's independent State Auditor, the state's nonpartisan fiscal watchdog, and shared broadly with the public, including in the Voter Information Guide. The financial and performance audits must:
Track all program spending and assess whether it's achieving its intended outcomes;
Determine whether programs have sufficient oversight and accountability;
Identify areas of waste, fraud and abuse; and,
Recommend how future waste and fraud can be avoided and how programs can be made more effective.
Under Prop 41, the Auditor is required to review programs funded by proposed new tax measures before voters cast their ballots and conduct ongoing audits if those measures are approved.
Q: What happens if an audit finds problems?
A: If the State Auditor identifies concerns about oversight, accountability or program performance, those findings are included in the Voter Information Guide so voters can make a more informed decision.
If a measure is approved, future audits continue evaluating how funds are spent, identify areas for improvement, and recommend ways to make programs more effective over time - so that programs are held accountable to the people who pay for them: taxpayers.
The audit doesn't decide whether a measure passes or fails; it gives voters independent information before they cast their ballot.
Q: What does Prop 41 mean for education, healthcare and other public programs?
A: Every tax dollar we waste is a dollar that could actually help someone. Prop 41 is built to sustain fiscal discipline alongside public investment. It does not cut or eliminate funding for education, healthcare or other public services, and it helps ensure that programs funded by taxpayers are transparent, accountable and delivering results. We deserve better services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Prop 41 requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, like homelessness (https://www.yesonprop41.org/homelessness) , so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Q: Does Prop 41 make it harder for initiatives to qualify for the ballot?
A: No. Prop 41 does not change the initiative process or prevent measures from qualifying for the ballot. Supporters can still gather signatures, qualify initiatives and campaign for their proposals just as they do today.
The difference is that under Prop 41, programs to be funded by new taxes are assessed before voters cast their ballot. The Auditor's findings must be posted in the Voter Information Guide, so voters have access to independent information about how programs are being managed and whether they actually need more funding. Voters deserve the ability to make informed decisions about new taxes without having to rely on information from special interests or politicians.
Q: Who pays for the audits?
A: If a tax measure is approved, the cost of the required audits is paid from the revenues generated by that measure. If voters reject the measure, the audit costs are paid through the state's General Fund.
Many statewide tax measures raise hundreds of millions - or even billions - of dollars over time. Prop 41 ensures a small investment in independent oversight helps taxpayers know whether those dollars are being spent effectively and producing the results promised.
Q: Who supports Prop 41?
Prop 41 is backed by a board coalition of small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, accountants, and auditing experts. Endorsers include the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, former State Controller Steve Westly, former California Auditor General Tom Hayes, the NAACP California-Hawaii State Conference, the California Alliance of Seniors, the California Chamber of Commerce, the California Farm Bureau, the California Taxpayers Association, the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, along with dozens of local chambers, taxpayer associations, and regional economic partnerships across the state.
Endorsements also include Democratic organizations and officials. The Chinese American Democratic Club, the San Bernardino Young Democrats, and the Sacramento State College Democrats have endorsed Prop 41, as has Steve Westly, a Democrat who served as State Controller. Local officials who have endorsed include Riverside County Auditor-Controller Ben Benoit and council members and mayors from across California. The full and current list of endorsers is at yesonprop41.org/endorsements (https://www.yesonprop41.org/endorsements) .
Q: How does Prop 41 strengthen taxpayer protections?
A: Prop 41 requires all future state tax measures to comply with California's voter-approved constitutional spending limit. That means future measures must follow the same constitutional rules that already apply to state spending including the requirement that excess revenues be refunded to taxpayers when the spending limit is exceeded.
Prop 41 provides for consistent application of the spending limit, so future state tax measures follow the same constitutional rules that already govern state spending, including the requirement that excess revenues be refunded to taxpayers.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
**Evaluating audit measures**

I’m considering various audit measures, particularly how many sources we have—20—and whether that's enough for a thorough investigation. I want to think clearly and not rush to conclusions; we could investigate if auditors can fulfill public requests for audits without needing a constitutional amendment. There are complexities with tax exemptions and state healthcare implications. I also reflect on the inefficiency of a binding 10% criterion and want to ensure I'm not overly reliant on donor information when making legal claims.**Analyzing growth and tax implications**

I’m looking at annual growth, which is around 79% compared to 2019, accounting for nominal changes over seven years—about 8.6%. However, when considering population decline and inflation of 30%, the real growth becomes 38%. It seems like there's a risk in further entrenching caps based on outdated baselines from 1978. I want to avoid any bias from the status quo regarding voters’ rights to decide on future taxes. Prop 41 requires amendments to create future exclusions, which complicates things.

content.text:
We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.
California has changed radically since the 1970s. And its fiscal rules must leave the state with the flexibility to address issues voters of the era never had to deal with — six-figure college costs, seven-figure mortgages and 13-figure wildfire costs.
The state must not surrender its future freedom of action to defeat a single, one-time tax proposal.
Proposition 42
This initiative would prohibit the state from taxing retroactively. And it would permanently ban the state from any new taxes on ownership of financial assets or other personal properties — think stocks, bonds, intellectual property, artwork, etc.
Taxes on wealth are rarely ideal, and our opposition to Proposition 40 reflects that.
However, we are witnessing an explosion of inequality, and the unpredictable course of AI’s development risks supercharging the gap between the haves and have-nots. Joint Venture Silicon Valley’s latest research shows that 78% of Bay Area residents are concerned AI will increase economic inequality.
Proposition 42 was written by this tech boom’s beneficiaries, who are now among the wealthiest humans in history. If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could have supported it. However, amid this era’s technology- and climate-induced uncertainty, California must keep its options open.
Proposition 42 would needlessly and recklessly narrow them.
Reject Propositions 40, 41 and 42.

California voters will soon decide whether to tax billionaires — but even if a majority says yes, the measure could still lose to either of two billionaire-funded measures designed to cancel it out. The billionaire-backed group Building a Better California designed two countermeasures to undermine the wealth tax and create multiple ways to defeat it. Recent polling shows slim majorities of likely voters support not just the wealth tax, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), but also Propositions 41 and 42, the measures aimed at killing it, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). “I don’t think that people at this point realize they’re direct countermeasures because there hasn’t been much said about 41 and 42,” said Mark Baldassare, polling director for PPIC. Only one outcome can prevail. If Prop. 40 captures more votes than both 41 and 42, the wealth tax takes effect, voiding the countermeasures. If either 41 or 42 outpolls Prop. 40, the billionaire tax does not take effect. What each measure does Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on California residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply based on residency as of Jan. 1, 2026 — a date that had passed when the measure qualified for the ballot — meaning billionaires who left the state afterward would still owe it. Most of the money generated would fund healthcare, while a smaller portion would go to education. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponent and financial backer of the measure, says the tax would raise about $100 billion and is needed to backfill federal healthcare cuts passed last year. Conservatives argue California’s Medi-Cal program has grown too expensive, and new federal policies will help the state cut back. Prop. 41’s real target is Prop. 40: It would require new tax proposals passed after the start of this year to follow the state’s annual spending limit — a cap passed by voters in 1979 (https://apnews.com/article/california-health-coronavirus-pandemic-business-personal-taxes-228c115a231bcc8ec000c7445e83d8e7) during a period of strong anti-tax sentiment that recent voter-approved special taxes have exempted themselves from. The billionaire tax would automatically violate this provision because it isn’t written to comply with the state spending limit. Prop 41 would also require the nonpartisan state auditor to review new tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. If voters approve a tax, some of the revenue generated would pay for the audit; if a proposal fails, the state would be on the hook for the additional cost. Prop. 42 would bar new taxes on personal property such as businesses, investments, retirement accounts, trusts and art collections — the exact things that Prop. 40 targets. It would also prohibit retroactive taxes, which would block a key part of Prop. 40: taxing wealth accumulated before the measure takes effect. Either provision alone is enough to nullify Prop. 40, if the wealth tax wins fewer votes than 41 or 42. “Prop. 42 is a more direct anti-wealth tax proposal,” said Megan Jones, a tax attorney with Holland and Knight. The Legislature has tried unsuccessfully in the past to pass multiple wealth taxes (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/tax-pros/law/legislation/2023-2024/AB259-011923.pdf), Jones said. If Prop. 42 passes, she said, it could limit lawmakers’ ability to try again in the future. Who’s funding the fights Backers of the billionaire tax — primarily SEIU-UHW — have raised about $31 million to pass the measure, mostly from union coffers. The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) also supports the measure. Prop 41 would put revenue from new state taxes under the Gann Limit’s rigid constitutional spending cap, making it harder to fund essential services and respond to changing needs.

***Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter Initiative Process.*** Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would receive funds from a new or increased special tax proposed through the voter initiative process.
This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a measure for the ballot, which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the ballot.
Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor would include in these audits, including identifying ways to reduce an audited program’s annual costs by 10 percent.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to write a summary of each audit.

Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.
California has changed radically since the 1970s. And its fiscal rules must leave the state with the flexibility to address issues voters of the era never had to deal with — six-figure college costs, seven-figure mortgages and 13-figure wildfire costs.
The state must not surrender its future freedom of action to defeat a single, one-time tax proposal.
Proposition 42
This initiative would prohibit the state from taxing retroactively. And it would permanently ban the state from any new taxes on ownership of financial assets or other personal properties — think stocks, bonds, intellectual property, artwork, etc.
Taxes on wealth are rarely ideal, and our opposition to Proposition 40 reflects that.
However, we are witnessing an explosion of inequality, and the unpredictable course of AI’s development risks supercharging the gap between the haves and have-nots. Joint Venture Silicon Valley’s latest research shows that 78% of Bay Area residents are concerned AI will increase economic inequality.
Proposition 42 was written by this tech boom’s beneficiaries, who are now among the wealthiest humans in history. If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could have supported it. However, amid this era’s technology- and climate-induced uncertainty, California must keep its options open.
Proposition 42 would needlessly and recklessly narrow them.
Reject Propositions 40, 41 and 42.

California voters will soon decide whether to tax billionaires — but even if a majority says yes, the measure could still lose to either of two billionaire-funded measures designed to cancel it out. The billionaire-backed group Building a Better California designed two countermeasures to undermine the wealth tax and create multiple ways to defeat it. Recent polling shows slim majorities of likely voters support not just the wealth tax, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), but also Propositions 41 and 42, the measures aimed at killing it, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). “I don’t think that people at this point realize they’re direct countermeasures because there hasn’t been much said about 41 and 42,” said Mark Baldassare, polling director for PPIC. Only one outcome can prevail. If Prop. 40 captures more votes than both 41 and 42, the wealth tax takes effect, voiding the countermeasures. If either 41 or 42 outpolls Prop. 40, the billionaire tax does not take effect. What each measure does Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on California residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply based on residency as of Jan. 1, 2026 — a date that had passed when the measure qualified for the ballot — meaning billionaires who left the state afterward would still owe it. Most of the money generated would fund healthcare, while a smaller portion would go to education. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponent and financial backer of the measure, says the tax would raise about $100 billion and is needed to backfill federal healthcare cuts passed last year. Conservatives argue California’s Medi-Cal program has grown too expensive, and new federal policies will help the state cut back. Prop. 41’s real target is Prop. 40: It would require new tax proposals passed after the start of this year to follow the state’s annual spending limit — a cap passed by voters in 1979 (https://apnews.com/article/california-health-coronavirus-pandemic-business-personal-taxes-228c115a231bcc8ec000c7445e83d8e7) during a period of strong anti-tax sentiment that recent voter-approved special taxes have exempted themselves from. The billionaire tax would automatically violate this provision because it isn’t written to comply with the state spending limit. Prop 41 would also require the nonpartisan state auditor to review new tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. If voters approve a tax, some of the revenue generated would pay for the audit; if a proposal fails, the state would be on the hook for the additional cost. Prop. 42 would bar new taxes on personal property such as businesses, investments, retirement accounts, trusts and art collections — the exact things that Prop. 40 targets. It would also prohibit retroactive taxes, which would block a key part of Prop. 40: taxing wealth accumulated before the measure takes effect. Either provision alone is enough to nullify Prop. 40, if the wealth tax wins fewer votes than 41 or 42. “Prop. 42 is a more direct anti-wealth tax proposal,” said Megan Jones, a tax attorney with Holland and Knight. The Legislature has tried unsuccessfully in the past to pass multiple wealth taxes (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/tax-pros/law/legislation/2023-2024/AB259-011923.pdf), Jones said. If Prop. 42 passes, she said, it could limit lawmakers’ ability to try again in the future. Who’s funding the fights Backers of the billionaire tax — primarily SEIU-UHW — have raised about $31 million to pass the measure, mostly from union coffers. The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) also supports the measure. The billionaire tax could be defeated by two other tax measures. Here’s how

By Kristen Hwang, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will soon decide whether to tax billionaires — but even if a majority says yes, the measure could still lose to either of two billionaire-funded measures designed to cancel it out. 

The billionaire-backed group Building a Better California designed two countermeasures to undermine the wealth tax and create multiple ways to defeat it.

Recent polling shows slim majorities of likely voters support not just the wealth tax, Proposition 40, but also Propositions 41 and 42, the measures aimed at killing it, according to the Public Policy Institute of California. 

“I don’t think that people at this point realize they're direct countermeasures because there hasn't been much said about 41 and 42,” said Mark Baldassare, polling director for PPIC.

Only one outcome can prevail. If Prop. 40 captures more votes than both 41 and 42, the wealth tax takes effect, voiding the countermeasures. If either 41 or 42 outpolls Prop. 40, the billionaire tax does not take effect.

What each measure does

Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on California residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply based on residency as of Jan. 1, 2026 — a date that had passed when the measure qualified for the ballot — meaning billionaires who left the state afterward would still owe it. 

Most of the money generated would fund healthcare, while a smaller portion would go to education. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponent and financial backer of the measure, says the tax would raise about $100 billion and is needed to backfill federal healthcare cuts passed last year. Conservatives argue California’s Medi-Cal program has grown too expensive, and new federal policies will help the state cut back. 

Prop. 41’s real target is Prop. 40: It would require new tax proposals passed after the start of this year to follow the state’s annual spending limit — a cap passed by voters in 1979 during a period of strong anti-tax sentiment that recent voter-approved special taxes have exempted themselves from. The billionaire tax would automatically violate this provision because it isn’t written to comply with the state spending limit.

Prop 41 would also require the nonpartisan state auditor to review new tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. If voters approve a tax, some of the revenue generated would pay for the audit; if a proposal fails, the state would be on the hook for the additional cost.

Prop. 42 would bar new taxes on personal property such as businesses, investments, retirement accounts, trusts and art collections — the exact things that Prop. 40 targets. It would also prohibit retroactive taxes, which would block a key part of Prop. 40: taxing wealth accumulated before the measure takes effect. Either provision alone is enough to nullify Prop. 40, if the wealth tax wins fewer votes than 41 or 42.

content.thinking:
**Evaluating audit measures**

I’m considering various audit measures, particularly how many sources we have—20—and whether that's enough for a thorough investigation. I want to think clearly and not rush to conclusions; we could investigate if auditors can fulfill public requests for audits without needing a constitutional amendment. There are complexities with tax exemptions and state healthcare implications. I also reflect on the inefficiency of a binding 10% criterion and want to ensure I'm not overly reliant on donor information when making legal claims.**Analyzing growth and tax implications**

I’m looking at annual growth, which is around 79% compared to 2019, accounting for nominal changes over seven years—about 8.6%. However, when considering population decline and inflation of 30%, the real growth becomes 38%. It seems like there's a risk in further entrenching caps based on outdated baselines from 1978. I want to avoid any bias from the status quo regarding voters’ rights to decide on future taxes. Prop 41 requires amendments to create future exclusions, which complicates things.

League Women Voters California 2026 "Proposition 41" audits

content.text:
We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.
California has changed radically since the 1970s. And its fiscal rules must leave the state with the flexibility to address issues voters of the era never had to deal with — six-figure college costs, seven-figure mortgages and 13-figure wildfire costs.
The state must not surrender its future freedom of action to defeat a single, one-time tax proposal.
Proposition 42
This initiative would prohibit the state from taxing retroactively. And it would permanently ban the state from any new taxes on ownership of financial assets or other personal properties — think stocks, bonds, intellectual property, artwork, etc.
Taxes on wealth are rarely ideal, and our opposition to Proposition 40 reflects that.
However, we are witnessing an explosion of inequality, and the unpredictable course of AI’s development risks supercharging the gap between the haves and have-nots. Joint Venture Silicon Valley’s latest research shows that 78% of Bay Area residents are concerned AI will increase economic inequality.
Proposition 42 was written by this tech boom’s beneficiaries, who are now among the wealthiest humans in history. If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could have supported it. However, amid this era’s technology- and climate-induced uncertainty, California must keep its options open.
Proposition 42 would needlessly and recklessly narrow them.
Reject Propositions 40, 41 and 42.

California voters will soon decide whether to tax billionaires — but even if a majority says yes, the measure could still lose to either of two billionaire-funded measures designed to cancel it out. The billionaire-backed group Building a Better California designed two countermeasures to undermine the wealth tax and create multiple ways to defeat it. Recent polling shows slim majorities of likely voters support not just the wealth tax, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), but also Propositions 41 and 42, the measures aimed at killing it, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). “I don’t think that people at this point realize they’re direct countermeasures because there hasn’t been much said about 41 and 42,” said Mark Baldassare, polling director for PPIC. Only one outcome can prevail. If Prop. 40 captures more votes than both 41 and 42, the wealth tax takes effect, voiding the countermeasures. If either 41 or 42 outpolls Prop. 40, the billionaire tax does not take effect. What each measure does Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on California residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply based on residency as of Jan. 1, 2026 — a date that had passed when the measure qualified for the ballot — meaning billionaires who left the state afterward would still owe it. Most of the money generated would fund healthcare, while a smaller portion would go to education. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponent and financial backer of the measure, says the tax would raise about $100 billion and is needed to backfill federal healthcare cuts passed last year. Conservatives argue California’s Medi-Cal program has grown too expensive, and new federal policies will help the state cut back. Prop. 41’s real target is Prop. 40: It would require new tax proposals passed after the start of this year to follow the state’s annual spending limit — a cap passed by voters in 1979 (https://apnews.com/article/california-health-coronavirus-pandemic-business-personal-taxes-228c115a231bcc8ec000c7445e83d8e7) during a period of strong anti-tax sentiment that recent voter-approved special taxes have exempted themselves from. The billionaire tax would automatically violate this provision because it isn’t written to comply with the state spending limit. Prop 41 would also require the nonpartisan state auditor to review new tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. If voters approve a tax, some of the revenue generated would pay for the audit; if a proposal fails, the state would be on the hook for the additional cost. Prop. 42 would bar new taxes on personal property such as businesses, investments, retirement accounts, trusts and art collections — the exact things that Prop. 40 targets. It would also prohibit retroactive taxes, which would block a key part of Prop. 40: taxing wealth accumulated before the measure takes effect. Either provision alone is enough to nullify Prop. 40, if the wealth tax wins fewer votes than 41 or 42. “Prop. 42 is a more direct anti-wealth tax proposal,” said Megan Jones, a tax attorney with Holland and Knight. The Legislature has tried unsuccessfully in the past to pass multiple wealth taxes (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/tax-pros/law/legislation/2023-2024/AB259-011923.pdf), Jones said. If Prop. 42 passes, she said, it could limit lawmakers’ ability to try again in the future. Who’s funding the fights Backers of the billionaire tax — primarily SEIU-UHW — have raised about $31 million to pass the measure, mostly from union coffers. The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) also supports the measure. ***State Appropriations Limit Poses Major Risk to Budget Multiyear Condition.*** The May Revision anticipates the state will collect $16 billion in revenues in excess of the SAL.
Our recent analysis suggests this is likely to continue to occur; however, the extent to which it does depends on many factors, including future decisions by the Legislature.
Consequently, this analysis does not attempt to calculate the amount of possible excess revenues in future years.
Under the Governor’s May Revision proposals, however, in future years, the state could collect revenues in excess of the SAL, but not have a surplus.
If that occurred, the state would need to make cuts to existing programs in order to meet its constitutional requirements.
This possibility poses a *major* risk to the multiyear budget condition and the state’s ability to pay for the level of services proposed in the May Revision.
